title: Private investment along Kerala coast: Could CM Satheesan convincingly allay concerns?
content: Thiruvananthapuram: Corporatisation, or the tweaking of government policies to suit corporate interests, is the most widely used term by the LDF to attack the VD Satheesan government. The Chief Minister, in turn, attempts to neutralise the charge by making fun of it, by making the LDF indictment sound like a joke. "When I scanned through the notice, I was surprised at the absence of a word," the CM began his reply to the adjournment motion on KIIFB moved by the LDF in the Assembly early on Wednesday. "But I was relieved on reading the explanatory note. Agenda of corporatisation!," he said with a look that said that there was no point in reasoning with such people. Later in the day, while replying to the discussion on the Kerala Maritime Board (Amendment) Bill, 2026, he said: "Whatever you say, they come up with the word corporatisation. Kerala is fed up of hearing the word corporatisation. These are the very same people who had organised an investors meet to invite corporates to Kerala". He was responding to Opposition Leader Pinarayi Vijayan's remark that the Maritime Board (Amendment) Bill was a consent letter placed before the corporate mafia to exploit the mineral wealth of Kerala's coast as they wish. Saying this, Pinarayi declared the boycott of the further proceedings related to the passage of the Bill. The Chief Minister said that private investment was inevitable. "Can any government develop our 18 mini ports by its own? We need private investment," he said. The Chief Minister also laughed away the charge of mineral loot by private companies. "There is no mention of minerals in this Act. More importantly, mining of minerals can be done only in the public sector," the CM said. He also listed the activities that would be encouraged by the Maritime Board, all of which he said would generate employment. Harbour development, Maritime industry, Maritime logistics, Container stations, Bunkering, Freight forwarding, Transhipment, Cargo movements, Warehouses, Supply chains, Facilities for the export of Kerala's value-added products like spices and marine items. Nonetheless, there were certain other issues related to the Maritime Board Act that the LDF members had raised for which the Chief Minister was unable to provide satisfactory answers. Land bank puzzle A primary concern related to the formation of a 'Maritime Land Bank'. CPM leader and former finance minister KN Balagopal said that once the Act all lands along the coast would have to be mandatorily handed over to the Land Bank. "Any land that is licked by water, in the custody of whichever department, will fall within the ambit of the Maritime Land Bank," he said, and added: "This is an enabling provision law that will necessitate the transfer of lands from other departments like revenue to the Maritime Board for its various uses, including for commercial purposes. Such a provision is liable to be misused," he said. The Chief Minister ridiculed the argument. "When you read a section in the Act, it should be read fully," the CM said and pointed to clause 3 of the amended section 22A. "It clearly states that lands within the Maritime Land Bank fall within port limits. Does it mean that the Board will take over all the government lands along the Kerala coast," he said. "Shouldn't we acquire lands that fall within the port limits? It is where development will take place," the CM said. Nonetheless, there is an element of justification in the concern raised by Balagopal. The same Clause also states that even if only within port limits, these could also be lands currently in the possession of other government departments like revenue and fisheries. So, as Balagopal said, lands with other Departments will also be taken over by the Maritime Board. What about title deeds for fishers Now, the question was how much land will be taken over...
